did_you_know.text: The word “Hebrews” is an ancient name for the Israelites, often used when outsiders are speaking about them. “Children of Israel” is a more national and family-based designation.
The list includes horses, donkeys, camels, cattle, and sheep—nearly all the main types of livestock in the ancient world. This shows that the loss was also a serious economic blow.
“Kiln soot” is dust or ash collected from a large furnace. Here, an ordinary handful of it becomes the sign of a widespread plague.
The magicians were religious and court officials regarded as experts in magic and healing. Their illness keeps them from even standing before Moses, undermining their authority.
The phrase “to your heart” refers not only to feelings but also to a person’s will and decisions. The struggle in this chapter is therefore also about Pharaoh’s inner stance.
A clear warning is given before the hail, so people have a chance to choose how to respond. In a story of plagues, the verse also emphasizes personal responsibility.
The description combines thunder, hail, and fire—an intense, vivid picture of a violent storm. It presents the storm as an especially terrifying natural force.
Moses says that the end of the storm will show that “the earth belongs to the Lord.” This expresses a broad idea: God’s rule is not limited to one land or one people.
Moses knows that ending the punishment will not yet bring a true change of heart in Pharaoh and his officials. Sometimes people acknowledge danger only while it is happening.
The verse reflects the growing seasons in Egypt: the barley was already ripening, and the flax was flowering. Flax was used to make fibers and clothing, so it was an important crop as well.
Wheat and spelt ripen later than barley, so they had not yet been damaged. These agricultural details help the reader understand both the timing and the extent of the destruction.
The rain and hail stop, but the relief leads Pharaoh to change his mind again. It is a familiar human pattern: during a crisis people promise to change, then return to old habits afterward.
